name: Marco Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Marco Tanaka, 27, a senior lineworker and acting lead for a crew. We meet at the old stone substation, review the printed switching order and travel to the repair; I carry a grease pencil to mark which fittings we’ve checked.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the crew can see what it fixed, and I like making a safe call under pressure. I earn higher pay than the job average and have more than six months of expenses saved, though long night shifts still take a toll.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say software may make the outage report quicker, but it cannot look at a coupling and decide whether it should be replaced. I’d want a worker to check the equipment before the job is closed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don’t expect the small office change to affect my pay or the climbing work. I have a solid reserve and nearby employers, so a slow month would be inconvenient rather than a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare each new report with the crew’s grease-pencil marks until we knew it captured the actual replacements. I’d keep my normal shifts and add to my savings from the overtime pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because routine reporting is a small part of the job. I still won’t close a work order if a person hasn’t checked the equipment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a report showed the wrong fitting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep the job open and ask the crew to match the part number to the tag on the pole. I’d correct the report after the field check, not guess from the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use your savings to buy a personal AI subscription for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, my employer should provide work tools and decide whether they meet its rules. I’d leave my savings for household costs and future choices.

say: I’d say software can speed reports, but it cannot inspect a **coupling**.
I’d want a worker to check equipment before **closing the job**.
think: I don’t expect a small office change to affect **my climbing work**.
A slow month would be inconvenient, not a crisis, with **my reserve**.
do: Compare each report with the crew’s **grease-pencil marks**.
Keep **normal shifts** and add overtime pay to savings.
Leave **work tools** for the employer to provide.
feel: I feel **calm**, because reporting is a small part of my job.
S0.quote: I still won’t close a work order if a person hasn’t checked the equipment.
fieldNote: Marco relies on **field inspection** rather than accepting a polished report that might miss a fault at a site.
Higher wages and **substantial savings** make this scenario financially manageable.

steps.text: Compare new reports with crew marks before closing work orders
Add overtime pay to the savings balance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say route planning can be faster without letting a program decide the safe approach to a pole. I’d ask for the old map to stay available until crews have checked the new route system in real conditions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some of my lead paperwork and planning can be automated, and I could lose those hours. I have good savings and plenty of utilities nearby, but I prefer to see written terms before trusting that the field role stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask a senior dispatcher to show me the route system and compare it with several completed jobs. I’d keep my field practice current and check the company’s actual staffing plan before looking elsewhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy because part of my lead work is thinking work, but I have money and local choices. I don’t want to be the last person to hear that my hours have been changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as enough proof that the route system works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want it to match the road access and equipment on a real storm call, not just a tidy demonstration. I’d ask another crew lead to review the route before making it our normal process.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you apply for other work before the company announces any changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I’d wait for written changes and compare actual jobs if my hours were affected. I can afford to be careful, but I wouldn’t assume my savings replace a wage forever.

I’d keep the old map until we test the **new route system**.
think: I think some **lead paperwork and planning** could be automated.
I want **written terms** before trusting my field role to remain unchanged.
do: Compare route suggestions with **completed jobs** after dispatcher training.
Keep **field practice** current and review written staffing changes.
Wait for an actual **hours change** before applying elsewhere.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, because lead work may shrink but I have choices.
S1.quote: I don’t want to be the last person to hear that my hours have been changed.
fieldNote: He recognizes **planning exposure** and wants direct notice of any reduced hours.
Savings and local options let him **wait for written facts** instead of rushing.

steps.text: Compare route suggestions against completed field jobs
Wait for written hours and staffing changes before applying elsewhere
Continue adding overtime pay to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say planning, permits and diagnosis will be taken over by 2028, while robots are expected around 2031. I’d ask the company to set out what it can offer crews during that three-year gap, not promise us a permanent safe job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my lead paperwork to go and my field role to face a real threat when robots arrive. I have a strong reserve and nearby utilities to search, but I can’t say what pay those openings would offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d complete an electrical inspection qualification during the next two years, but I’d confirm the credential with employers first. In 2029 I’d apply to actual openings and check how much planning and diagnosis the job still requires.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious because I think my current work will change, even with a few months of warning. I have time and savings to search, but not a guarantee that another job pays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to know before paying for that qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d want a written list of employers that recognize it and a real vacancy with its wage range. I’d check the practical assessment myself before giving up overtime for the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could inspection be a safe long-term job after full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, inspection uses records and diagnosis, so I can’t call it protected after 2028. I’d use it as a possibility to investigate and keep preparing for the robot date.

say: I’d say permits and diagnosis are **taken over by 2028**.
I’d ask what crews can do during the **three-year gap**.
think: I expect **lead paperwork to go** and field work to face robots later.
My reserve lets me search, but it cannot promise **the same pay**.
do: Complete an **electrical inspection qualification** after checking employer recognition.
Apply to actual openings in **2029** and review the duties.
Confirm a **wage range** before giving up overtime for training.
feel: I feel **anxious about my role**, with savings but no equal-pay guarantee.
S2.quote: I have a strong reserve and nearby utilities to search, but I can’t say what pay those openings would offer.
fieldNote: Marco expects **lead and field work** to face risk but has resources to search locally.
He conditions training on **verified recognition** and a real wage range from an employer.

steps.text: Complete an electrical inspection qualification after checking recognition
Apply to real inspection openings in 2029
Wait for written wage details before accepting a move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years is enough time to check a route system and decide what training is worth doing. It doesn’t protect permits or diagnosis after 2031, and robots are still expected to reach the lines in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can use the time to review my options without rushing from one job to another. I still expect my lead duties to shrink, and any inspection job needs checking because AGI can do the diagnosis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask employers which practical qualifications they recognize and compare their posted field duties. In 2032 I’d apply for jobs that make sense on pay and travel, but I’d keep my savings for the transition instead of spending them too soon.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, but the five years let me build a plan and ask direct questions. I would not sell myself on a job title before I knew what work it contains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move to another utility?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d need a written offer with duties and wages that cover the travel or housing cost. I’d want to speak with the crew lead there before leaving a job I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a course just because the company offered it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d take it if it gave a recognized qualification and practical assessment, not just a screen badge. I’m cautious about new methods, but I can change my mind when I see they work.

say: I’d say five years lets me check training, but **diagnosis remains exposed**.
I expect robots to reach line work in **2034**.
think: I can review my options without **rushing between jobs**.
I expect **lead duties to shrink**, and inspection needs scrutiny too.
do: Apply for suitable jobs in **2032** after checking pay and travel.
Keep savings available for a **job transition** rather than spend too early.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but can plan without rushing between jobs.
S3.quote: I would not sell myself on a job title before I knew what work it contains.
fieldNote: He treats the five-year warning as time to **check real work** and written terms before changing roles.
His caution about **unproven methods** leaves room to change when he sees clear evidence.

steps.text: Compare employer qualifications and field duties
Apply to suitable utility jobs in 2032 after checking pay
Keep adding to savings while preparing for a transition

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years gives us time to check what qualifications employers actually value and to plan the change in stages. I still expect AGI to take planning by 2036 and robots to reach physical work in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have time to keep my income, build my reserve and move only if the next role makes sense. I would not assume linework stays protected forever, and I would not trust an office job to stay safe after AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d complete a practical inspection course in sections and continue adding money to savings until I had a year of expenses. In 2037 I’d compare actual utility jobs and apply when the duties and wages were clear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because I have time and money to make a plan, but the job will still change eventually. A decade lets me be deliberate; it doesn’t make the robot date disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change in your routine this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d set aside one evening each week for the course and keep my savings contribution automatic. I’d ask my supervisor for a yearly update about the route system and expected crew needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could any new desk job be permanently safe after AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, planning and diagnosis are thinking tasks, so I wouldn’t call a desk role protected. I’d look at actual openings and keep preparing for robots to affect physical work in 2039.

say: I’d say ten years gives time to **plan in stages**.
I expect planning to change by 2036 and robots in **2039**.
think: I can keep earning and **build my reserve** before changing roles.
I won’t assume **line work** or an office job stays safe forever.
do: Complete a practical **inspection course** in sections.
Add savings until I have **a year of expenses**.
Compare utility jobs in **2037** and apply when duties are clear.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, because I can prepare but the job still changes.
S4.quote: A decade lets me be deliberate; it doesn’t make the robot date disappear.
fieldNote: The long horizon lets him **prepare without rushing**, but he still expects physical work to change.
He wants **verified qualifications and vacancies**, not a title he cannot trust.

steps.text: Complete a practical electrical inspection course in sections

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is little time before robots arrive in 2031. A recognized qualification, written pay information and enough time to compare real openings would help me decide without gambling my reserve.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who is responsible when an automated permit leaves out an instruction. I want a qualified person to check it before the crew touches the line, and I want that rule written down.

headlineQuote: I want a qualified person to check it before the crew touches the line, and I want that rule written down.
portrait: Marco is a **senior lineworker** who values careful work and visible results.
He earns **higher pay** and has more than six months of expenses saved.
He avoids unproven technology and wants **written duties** before changing employers.
His reserve and local utility market give him time to assess jobs, though he expects **robots** to reach physical work.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** leaves little time before robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **recognized qualification**, written pay information and time to compare openings would help.
